rows.t: Wedding of the Winds Waltz  for Third Accordion Vintage Sheet Music John T Hall

det.desc: This is vintage sheet music for "Wedding of the Winds" Waltz, a famous concert waltz composed by John T. Hall (a pseudonym for John T. Newcomer, 1875–1954). The waltz was originally composed for piano around 1896 and published in various formats, including wind band and orchestra, by publishers like Carl Fischer and Jerome H. Remick & Co.. This specific piece is for the 3rd Accordion part, arranged by the renowned accordionist Anthony Galla-Rini. Galla-Rini was a prolific arranger who helped legitimize the accordion as a concert instrument. "Wedding of the Winds" became one of Hall's most enduring successes. It was famously recorded on Edison cylinders by early accordion pioneer Pietro Frosini in 1909. John T. Hall was a successful early 20th-century composer, but his career was also marked by a conviction for mail fraud in 1915 related to a "song-poem" publishing scam. Despite this, "Wedding of the Winds" remains a staple of light classical and accordion repertoire.

det.desc: CLEON PETERSON – "I AGAINST I" (WHITE) – 2026 – SIGNED & NUMBERED 9/75 About the Artist Cleon Peterson (b. 1973, Seattle) is a Los Angeles–based artist known for bold, graphic scenes of clashing figures locked in a struggle between power and submission. Trained in graphic design at Art Center College of Design and holding an MFA from Cranbrook Academy of Art, Peterson draws on the look of ancient Greek vase painting and propaganda posters, working in a stark, limited palette. His work has been shown at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Museum of Contemporary Art Denver, the Denver Art Museum, Kaikai Kiki in Tokyo, and Albertz Benda in New York, and he famously projected his work onto the Eiffel Tower for Nuit Blanche 2016. His limited-edition screen prints are widely collected and regularly sell out on release. About the Print "I Against I" shows two figures, one black and one metallic gold, wound together in a single knot of limbs, an embrace and a fight at the same time. It's a compact, powerful example of the push and pull between aggressor and victim that runs through Peterson's work.
